job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Dana Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet, honestly. I live in my parents' bungalow in Corvale, and I get up when Dad leaves for the depot at six. I studied business management, did six weeks at Tern and Hale, an insurance broker, filing claims and answering the phone. Now I work three days at the garden centre café, then spend the afternoon on job sites and writing letters that I print and post, because some firms still want that. Mum says I should relax, but I can't while the loan letters keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's more like the world I know. I'd tell Mum and Dad that it won't change much, and they'd nod. Online I wouldn't say anything, because I don't have opinions that fit in a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's the same problem as now. There are hardly any office jobs in Corvale, and the insurance firm where I interned has told me twice it isn't hiring. My loan is the size of a small house deposit, and I'm paying it with garden centre tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, but I'd also apply for jobs I'd normally skip, like the council records office and the bank branch in the next town. I'd ask Tern and Hale again in spring when their year starts. I'd keep the café hours, which are boring but steady, and I'd skip anything that costs money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat. It's not fear, just a grey feeling, like waiting at a bus stop where the bus may not come. Mum says I'm patient, but I think I'm just stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bank branch in the next town and the council records office specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're steady and they've been there forever. I know somebody's cousin at the council who said they do hire from time to time. A bank branch seems safe too, though I know branches are closing. I'd rather have a dull, stable job than a flashy one that vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if nothing turns up by the summer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask the café for full-time hours and put the degree away for a year, which I'd hate. I'd tell Dad I can't pay the room money for a few months, and he'd say fine, but I'd feel awful. I try not to think past the summer.

Online I'd say **nothing**, because my opinions don't fit in a post.
think: It's the **same problem** as now: almost no office jobs in Corvale.
My loan is the size of a small **house deposit**.
do: Apply to the council **records office** and the bank branch next town.
Ask Tern and Hale again in **spring**.
Keep the **café hours** and skip anything that costs money.
feel: **Flat** and grey, like waiting at a bus stop where the bus may not come.

fieldNote: Prefers **stable** and familiar over exciting, which matches her resistant side.

steps.text: Apply to the council records office and the bank branch next town
Ask Tern and Hale again about openings in spring
Keep the garden centre café hours
Skip anything that costs money until a job comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like a lot of fuss, and we'll see how it goes. At work, if I had one, I'd go along with whatever the firm decides. I'd tell friends I don't love it, because the entry jobs are the ones that go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, that list is my job: writing, checking, answering customers. At Tern and Hale I answered the phone and filed claims, and now I hear they're trialling a chatbot. I've never used one of these AI tools, and I'm behind and I know it. I'd say my chances of an office job in Corvale go from poor to very poor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with a friend who uses the tools and have them show me, once, slowly. I'd widen the search to the city, which means a long commute or a rented room, so I'd work out if the pay would cover it. And I'd ask the garden centre whether I could move up to supervisor, since that's a real job nobody is replacing soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit ashamed. I hate being behind on something everyone else seems to pick up. It's the sort of thing that makes me stay in on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does being behind on the tools bother you so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm already the last one to everything. My cousin Rhea uses them to write her CV in ten minutes, and mine takes a week. I don't want to be sitting at an interview admitting I've never tried it. It feels like I failed a test nobody told me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a supervisor job at the garden centre be a fall-back or a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. It's honest work and the manager seems to like me, but I didn't do a degree to count tills. If I'm honest, I'd take it for a couple of years and keep looking. At least it's steady money.

I'd tell friends I don't love it, since entry jobs go **first**.

Ask the garden centre about a **supervisor** role.

steps.text: Ask a friend to teach her one AI tool, slowly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to cope, and the government has to step in. I'd tell Mum and Dad not to spend on anything big. Online I'd probably just read, not post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm scared. Two years means I'm 25 with a degree for jobs that don't exist and a loan that does. I've never used the tools, so I'd be starting from a long way behind. I'd say my future gets decided by other people, and I have no say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every hour at the café and save as much as possible, because cash is what's left when jobs go. I'd ask my parents to hold on to the room money until we know what happens. And I'd visit the bank and the loan company to ask what they do if people can't pay, so I know before I need to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. My chest feels tight and I can't think past each week. I'd probably cry in the car park behind the café, then go back in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mum and Dad about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight that it isn't the sort of debt they can fix, and I don't want them selling the bungalow or borrowing for me. Dad would say don't worry, and I'd have to say I will anyway. It would be an awful talk, so I'd probably put it off for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2031. Would the café be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a bit, I think. Someone has to hand over the cake and wipe the tables, and people like a face. Then again, my cousin says there are robot cafés now, so maybe not forever. I'd treat the café as a bridge of a few years, not a plan.

S2.quote: Two years means I'm 25 with a degree for jobs that don't exist and a loan that does.
fieldNote: Feels decisions will be made **for her**, which deepens the fear.

steps.text: Take every café hour offered and save the extra
Ask the loan company what happens if payments stop
Ask parents to hold the room money until things are clearer
Cut every cost that isn't food, travel to interviews or loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more breathing room, and the government should use it. At home I'd say we should plan quietly, not panic. I'd tell friends to learn the tools while there's still time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years could be enough to get one proper job and keep it. The worry is that jobs vanish exactly when I'm getting settled. I'd also have my loan down by then, if I'm careful, so it's not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd find any office job, even a basic one, in a firm that looks like it'll last, such as the council. I'd learn the tools at work, one task at a time, with someone patient beside me. And I'd pay off my loan faster than I need to, so I'm lighter if things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, but not as tight in the chest. Five years feels like a stretch of road I can see most of. I'd still check my phone for job alerts at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would learning with someone patient beside you work better than a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I freeze when I'm alone with a screen and a video. If a person says click here, try this, I learn fine. At Tern and Hale a woman called Gwen showed me the claims system in two afternoons and I never forgot it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a firm that looks like it will last mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A council, a hospital office, a big insurer with many branches. Something where one bad year doesn't close the doors. I know nothing's certain, but I'd choose the dull and solid option every time.

I'd tell friends to **learn the tools** while there's time.

steps.text: Take any office job at a council or large insurer

Pay the student loan down faster than required
Plan quietly and avoid big purchases until the job is secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and people should stay calm. I'd tell my parents they'll be retired before it matters. At work, if I had work, I'd go with whatever training they offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, that's the first version where I think I'd be fine. In ten years I could have a decent job, a smaller loan and some savings. I'm not a person who jumps early, but with ten years I'd get there by walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job in a steady firm and learn it well. I'd take any training they give, even if it's about the AI tools, and do the evening course that Mum keeps cutting out of the paper. I'd save a bit each month and look at a deposit in maybe six or seven years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. There'd still be a small stone in my stomach, because I know I'm slow to change. But ten years feels like a big field to walk across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you worry about even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd leave learning to the last minute, the way I always do. If everyone else is using the tools for years and I only start in year nine, I'd be the odd one out. I'd have to set myself reminders and take small steps every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm applying, I'm working at the café, and I'm not going to waste the degree. I'd tell Mum she doesn't have to worry so much. She won't stop, but I'd say it anyway.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** of time and people should stay calm.
I'd go with whatever **training** an employer offers.
think: This is the first version where I think I'd be **fine**.
With ten years I'd get there by **walking**, not jumping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years gives me no time to catch up on anything. What would help is a job where someone patient teaches me, a way to pause my loan if I can't find work, and the government making sure the dull solid jobs, like council offices, keep hiring graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't asking for anything exciting. I'd just like a steady job, a safe loan and somebody to show me the tools once.

headlineQuote: I'd just like a steady job, a safe loan and somebody to show me the tools once.
portrait: Dana, 23, has a **good business degree**, six weeks at an insurance broker and three café days a week.
She lives with her parents, avoids AI tools and fears being the **last** to learn.
She is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road: she wants **stable**, dull employers and a person to teach her.
Her mood is anxious in most worlds because jobs are scarce and her loan is the size of a deposit.
Only ten years of warning lets her feel near **calm**, and she knows her habit of delay.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because two years gives her no time to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A job with a **patient teacher**, a way to pause the loan, and steady employers still hiring graduates.
